lessons.title: Key water quality parameters and what they mean
lessons.html:
Why we measure water quality

At supervisor level you are expected to go beyond looking and smelling. You measure specific parameters (properties of the water) and compare them with the target range for the use: livestock drinking, irrigation, washing produce, spray mixing or aquaculture.

The main parameters

ParameterWhat it tells you
pHHow acid or alkaline the water is. Affects nutrient uptake, drip system scaling and how well some pesticides work.
EC (electrical conductivity)A measure of dissolved salts. High EC can damage sensitive crops and reduce stock intake.
TemperatureAffects dissolved oxygen, fish health and algae growth.
Dissolved oxygenCritical in fish ponds and dams; low levels kill fish.
TurbidityCloudiness from suspended soil. Blocks filters and drippers and reduces spray effectiveness.
Microbial load (e.g. E. coli)Faecal contamination. Important for drinking water and water touching fresh produce.
Hardness, iron, manganeseCause scaling, staining and blocked emitters.

Target ranges

Target ranges depend on the use, the crop and the species. Use the ranges set by your farm manager, agronomist, vet or the relevant guidelines (such as the South African Water Quality Guidelines published by the Department of Water and Sanitation). Do not invent limits. If a reading is outside the range, report it and follow the action plan.

Instruments

  • Handheld pH and EC meters, which must be calibrated with buffer and standard solutions as the maker instructs
  • Thermometers and dissolved oxygen meters
  • Test strips and kits for quick checks
  • Laboratory analysis for microbes, heavy metals and full chemistry

Rinse probes with clean water after use, store them as instructed, and record each calibration. An uncalibrated meter gives readings that look precise but are wrong.

lessons.title: Sampling, recording and corrective action
lessons.html:
Taking a good sample

  1. Use clean containers; for lab samples, use the bottles the lab supplies.
  2. Label each sample: source, point, date, time and your name.
  3. Sample from the point of use (e.g. the trough, the dripper line or the wash bath), not only the source.
  4. Run taps for a short time before sampling a pipe.
  5. Keep lab samples cool and deliver them within the time the lab specifies.

Recording

Keep a water quality log for each source and point: date, parameter, reading, target range, who tested and action taken. Records show trends, for example EC rising in a borehole during drought, and they are required by many market and food safety audits.

Common problems and corrective actions

ProblemPossible actions
High turbiditySettle in a reservoir, improve filtration, protect catchment from erosion.
pH out of rangeAdjust with acid or alkali dosing as advised by an agronomist; use buffering agents for spray tanks per label.
High ECBlend with better water, change source, choose salt-tolerant crops, leach soils if drainage allows.
Algae in damsReduce nutrient run-off from fertiliser and manure; aerate.
Microbial contaminationStop use for drinking or produce, find the source, treat (e.g. approved chlorination) and retest before use.
Blocked drippersFlush lines, clean filters, acid treatment as advised.

Safety

Acids and chlorine products are hazardous. Wear the PPE on the label, always add acid to water and never water to acid, and store treatment chemicals locked away. Never let treatment chemicals or fertiliser enter rivers. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 governs water use and pollution of water resources.

Key points

  • Measure pH, EC, temperature, oxygen, turbidity and microbes as relevant to the use.
  • Use targets from your manager, adviser or official guidelines; never guess.
  • Calibrate meters and record every reading and action.
  • Sample at the point of use and label samples fully.
  • Fix the cause, then retest before returning water to use.
